note: 'Real boredom' defined as 'an unpleasant, transient affective state in which the individual feels a pervasive lack of interest in and difficulty concentrating on the current activity' (paraphrased; short direct fragment quoted), the sole definitional anchor for this paper's boredom condition (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.83).

Flow defined as 'the holistic sensation that people feel when they act with total involvement' (direct quote, 11 words), with characteristics: balance of challenge/skill, clear goals, explicit feedback, indistinct sense of time, loss of self-consciousness, enjoyment, control, autotelic activity (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.82).

target: Ellis et al. (1994) four-channel flow model
note: Revises Csikszentmihalyi's original flow model into a two-dimensional four-channel model (Fig.1: skill x challenge) yielding flow/anxiety/apathy/boredom quadrants -- boredom appears here as a named, structurally opposite quadrant to flow (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.82).

Primary theoretical anchor of the entire paper; Csikszentmihalyi's model + four-channel revision defined at length; GEQ flow subscale administered; flow-designed level scores highest on every physiological measure taken, described as 'high-arousal positive affect' (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.82, 86-87).

Boredom operationalized purely as a situational, experimentally-induced level condition identical across all 25 participants; no boredom-proneness or other trait instrument administered anywhere in the study (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.83).

Boredom-condition design criteria -- linear level, repeating textures/models, weak/repetitive opponents, damped sound, 'no real winning condition,' 'no surprises' -- operationally define monotony as the mechanism inducing the boredom condition (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.83).

Present only via the single borrowed Fisher (1993) definition's attentional-failure clause ('difficulty concentrating on the current activity'); never developed as an independent construct or measured directly (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.83).

GEQ (7 subscales) + MEC Spatial Presence Questionnaire (2 subscales) administered after each of 3 modality plays; analytic N approx 21 (inferred from ANOVA df); significant only for GEQ challenge/tension and both MEC-SPQ subscales (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.84-87).

target: facial electromyography (EMG) [own-term measure, no exact controlled-vocabulary match]
note: OO (positive valence), CS (negative valence), ZM (positive valence) via BioSemi electrodes, ActiveTwo AD-box 2kHz; analytic N approx 16 (inferred); OO and ZM significant (flow condition highest), CS non-significant; falls outside the twelve given MEASURE-axis columns and is logged under the source's own terminology (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.84-85, 87).

target: galvanic skin response (GSR) [own-term measure, no exact controlled-vocabulary match]
note: Log-transformed skin conductance via two passive Nihon Kohden electrodes on the left hand; analytic N approx 16 (inferred); significant, flow condition highest arousal; falls outside the twelve given MEASURE-axis columns and is logged under the source's own terminology (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.84, 87).

target: flow / engagement (contrast pole) <- self-report / survey scale (GEQ flow subscale)
note: GEQ flow subscale administered as the primary self-report index of the flow condition, though the subscale itself did not reach significance across the three conditions (F(2,40)=2.08, p>.05) despite the flow condition's other significant results elsewhere (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.86).

target: flow / engagement (contrast pole) <- facial EMG + GSR
note: The paper's own internal construct-measure pairing: flow's positive-valence high-arousal profile is operationalized via OO/ZM (valence) and GSR (arousal), the physiological triad that most clearly discriminated the flow condition from the other two (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.86-87).

target: situational vs. trait/state boredom <- self-report / survey scale (GEQ)
note: The boredom-designed level is operationalized/validated via GEQ scores: lowest on challenge/immersion/flow, highest on competence, 'completely in line with expectations' for a low-engagement condition (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.86).
The base game engine and content modified to create the three experimental level conditions (boredom, immersion, flow) (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.83).
Experiential Modes of Game Play; informs the demographic-data-collection design used in the Participants section (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.84).
A Grounded Investigation of Game Immersion; source of the engagement/engrossment/total-immersion (=presence) gradient discussed in section 1.1 (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.81).

Handbook of Psychophysiology / Psychophysiological Science; source of the 'many-to-one' mapping between psychological processing and physiological response underlying the paper's measurement rationale (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.82).
Flow in Games; source of the 'flow zones' concept for hardcore vs. novice players and an optimal challenge-skill intersection (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.82).
Beyond Boredom and Anxiety; origin of the flow model, its title itself pairing boredom and anxiety as flow's two failure modes (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.82).
Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience; the fuller statement of the flow model this paper adopts (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.82).

target: Ellis, G.D., Voelkl, J.E., and Morris, C. (1994) [ref.10]
note: Source of the four-channel revision of the flow model shown in Fig.1 (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.82).

Fundamental Components of the Gameplay Experience: Analysing Immersion; source of the sensory/challenge-based/imaginative (SCI) immersion typology and the finding that Half-Life 2 ranked highest on all SCI dimensions (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.81).
Boredom at Work: A Neglected Concept; the sole source of this paper's boredom definition (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.83).
Guidelines for Human Electromyographic Research; followed for facial-EMG recording-site selection (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.84).
The Acoustic Ecology of the First-Person Shooter; source of the 'virtual prostheses' framing for FPS weapons/hands as player-character extension (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.81).

target: IJsselsteijn, W.A., Poels, K., and de Kort, Y.A.W. [ref.15]
note: Measuring Player Experiences in Digital Games; developers of the Game Experience Questionnaire (GEQ), this paper's primary self-report instrument, developed under the EU FP6 FUGA project (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.82).

Development and Validation of a Scale to Measure Optimal Experience: The Flow State Scale; the only commonly used flow questionnaire prior to the GEQ, designed for sports research (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.82).
Psychophysiology of Flow Experience: An Explorative Study; assessed the Flow State Scale for game research usability; found no significant EMG-flow relationship (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.82).

This paper's own significant OO and ZM (positive-valence EMG) results across conditions, with flow scoring highest, directly contradict Kivikangas's (2006) prior finding of no significant relationship between zygomaticus/orbicularis EMG activity and flow (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.87).
The Emotion Probe; source of the dimensional (valence-arousal) theory of emotion grounding the EMG(valence)/GSR(arousal) measurement architecture (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.82).
Looking at Pictures: Affective, Facial, Visceral, and Behavioral Reactions; further grounding for the valence-arousal psychophysiological framework (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.82).
Direct Measurement of Skin Conductance: A Proposal for Standardization; methodological grounding for the GSR measurement (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.82).

Immersion, Engagement, and Presence: A New Method for Analyzing 3-D Video Games; cited on how player action's consequence and meaning within a game environment influence the feeling of immersion (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.81).

target: Nacke, L. and Lindley, C. (2008) [ref.22, self-citation, reversed author order]
note: This FuturePlay paper reports and extends the same underlying boredom/immersion/flow experiment first reported (GEQ results only, in more detail) as an IADIS 2008 pilot study by the same two authors, there ordered 'Nacke and Lindley' -- the reverse of this paper's own byline order (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.86).

target: Nacke, L., Lindley, C., and Stellmach, S. (2008) [ref.23]
note: Log Who's Playing: Psychophysiological Game Analysis Made Easy through Event Logging; cited as a related future-work direction for finer-grained, event-level analysis (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.83).

target: Novak, T.P., Hoffman, D.L., and Yung, Y.F. (2000) [ref.24]
note: Measuring the Flow Construct in Online Environments; survey finding 16 flow studies (1977-1996) using divergent concepts and definitions of flow, motivating this paper's own operationalization choices (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.82).

The Psychophysiology of Video Gaming / The Psychophysiology of James Bond; cited in support of the interpretation that challenging gameplay produces joy independent of victory or success (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.87).

Increased Oscillatory Theta Activation Evoked by Violent Digital Game Events; an EEG finding cited in the discussion of future directions, relevant to this paper's own unanalyzed EEG data (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.87).

MEC Spatial Presence Questionnaire (MECSPQ): Short Documentation and Instructions for Application; source of the spatial-presence self-report instrument administered alongside the GEQ (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.84).

target: self-report (GEQ) vs. psychophysiological (EMG/GSR) discrimination of gameplay experience
note: GEQ discriminated only 2 of 7 subscales (challenge, tension) while EMG/GSR discriminated 3 of 4 physiological channels (OO, ZM, GSR; not CS); the paper reads this as demonstrating physiological measures' potential relative to self-report alone, without fully reconciling why GEQ's own immersion/flow subscales underperformed (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.86-87).

All participants played boredom, immersion, and flow conditions in the same order; the authors judge the resulting learning-effect risk minor since the three experiential dimensions 'only marginally overlap,' an assumption asserted, not empirically tested (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.84).

target: own sample generalizability and preliminary study status
note: All-male, self-selected 'hardcore' gamer sample of unknown generalizability to a broader demographic; and an explicit footnote conceding the psychophysiological characterization of gameplay experience 'is not well developed, yet' (FAITHFUL-Nacke & Lindley, p.83, 87).

target: Boredom Experiment (VR Attention Study) -- self-report / survey engagement-flow channel
note: ****** UNVERIFIED: this paper's GEQ + MEC-SPQ self-report architecture (7 + 2 subscales, administered after each of several purpose-built experimental conditions within one platform) offers a reusable self-report-channel template for a future VR attention study contrasting engaging vs. boring/monotonous VLE content; the closest genuine controlled-vocabulary MEASURE match to this paper's own instrumentation, since its facial EMG/GSR measures fall outside the twelve given axis columns entirely. The dataset entry does not yet exist and its instrumentation is unconfirmed (P/anticipatory-application).

P/anticipatory-application -- this paper's method of manufacturing a low-engagement ('boredom') condition through concrete, replicable level-design features (linearity, repetition, absence of surprise/winning condition) within the same platform/content family as its high-engagement (flow) comparison condition is directly transferable to Part III's engagement-contrast design questions (desktop-3D vs. video-only strata; lab=VR/deployment=2D-PC poles), holding engine and sample constant across conditions.

target: caution re: EMG/GSR and small-N subgroup generalizability
note: P/anticipatory-application -- this paper's own analytic samples shrink substantially and unevenly by channel (N approx 21 self-report, N approx 16 physiological, from 25 recruited, inferred from reported degrees of freedom), its condition order was fixed rather than counterbalanced, and its sample was restricted to self-selected male hardcore gamers; any Part III or dataset design borrowing this triadic boredom/immersion/flow architecture should budget for comparable attrition, counterbalance condition order, and treat generalizability beyond a narrow player demographic as an open question.
